description: MBA Okulları Çamlıca Kampüsü tarafından imzalanan MBA Nox Team teknolojik ve yenilikçi projelerin geliştirilmesini sağlayan bir takımdır.
summary:
In Türkiye, farmers still decide what to plant, when to irrigate and when to apply crop protection based on past experience, yet the climate has changed: rising temperatures, irregular rainfall, more frequent droughts, frost and heatwaves, and spreading pests. 2025 was the driest year since 1964. NASA satellites observe every field daily and the data are open, but technical and fragmented, so they rarely reach farmers.

TerraShift AI addresses this gap by building a live digital twin of each field from NASA POWER and GIBS data. It jointly analyses more than 140 parameters, not a single variable, including temperature, precipitation, soil moisture, solar radiation, wind, frost and heat stress, drought indices, crop development, region-specific pest and disease risks, economic return and carbon impact. It warns farmers of emerging risks and compares 15 crops to recommend the most suitable crop and planting time, with transparent reasoning. Only the field’s location is required.

The twin is delivered through two interfaces. The Simple Panel serves farmers with limited literacy or digital experience: a traffic-light status, short daily actions in large text, read-aloud cards and voice questions in plain Turkish. The Advanced Panel serves agronomists and advisors with all parameters, a 3D field model, satellite and thermal maps, scenarios and a step-by-step reasoning module.

Our aim is to turn space data into one clear answer: what should I do for my field today?
details:
TerraShift AI is an AI-powered decision support system that transforms NASA’s open satellite and climate data into a working “digital twin” for every farm field. As soon as a user selects a field, the system uses its geographic coordinates to retrieve core daily climate variables from NASA POWER, including temperature, precipitation, root-zone and surface soil moisture, relative humidity, wind speed and direction, and solar radiation. In parallel, it retrieves satellite layers from NASA GIBS, such as MODIS true-colour imagery and land surface temperature, VIIRS, SMAP soil moisture, GPM precipitation and vegetation indices. The data refresh automatically every 15 minutes, and if the connection drops, the system continues to run on the most recently retrieved data and states this clearly on screen.

Behind the interface, a computational layer we call the “Mother AI” derives more than 140 field-level parameters from these raw data. Crop water demand is calculated using the internationally recognised FAO-56 Penman-Monteith method. Drought conditions are monitored through the SPI and KBDI indices, alongside frost and heat stress days, growing degree days and the field water balance. We also built nine separate pest and disease models, each reflecting threats that genuinely affect its region: European corn borer, cotton bollworm and aflatoxin risk for Çukurova, and sunn pest, yellow rust and pistachio psyllid for south-eastern Türkiye. The Mother AI evaluates all of these parameters together and scores 15 candidate crops against six criteria: water security, climate suitability, economic return, sustainability, risk and market. It then recommends the most suitable crop, planting window and multi-year rotation plan for that specific field.

Avoiding a “black box” was important to us, so we developed a reasoning module in which the AI displays every step it takes, from reading the data to reaching a decision. When users adjust the weighting of the criteria, or select a scenario such as drought, a heatwave or late frost, the system reasons again and revises its recommendation where necessary.

The “Child AI” is the layer that delivers this information to the farmer. Each farmer sees only the twin of their own field, through one of two interfaces. The Simple Panel is designed for farmers with limited literacy or digital experience. It communicates the field’s condition through a traffic-light indicator and answers the question “What should I do today?” in a few short sentences in large text. Every card can be read aloud, and farmers can ask questions by voice. The Advanced Panel is designed for agricultural engineers and advisors. It presents every parameter with its interpretation, together with a rotatable 3D model of the field and its soil layers, a 3D wind flow, thermal and satellite maps, a scenario laboratory and a screen comparing two farms side by side.

The project’s benefits emerge at several levels. For farmers, it means anticipating risks, reducing losses caused by unsuitable crops or poor timing, and protecting income. At the national level, it supports more efficient use of resources such as water, fertiliser and pesticides. Economically, the system estimates revenue, cost and carbon impact for each recommendation, which opens access to new income streams such as eco-premiums and carbon credits for farmers who adopt sustainable practices. According to our model calculations for the sample farms, switching a 40-hectare corn field in Çukurova to soybean saves approximately 78,000 cubic metres of water in one season while also increasing farm income. These figures are model estimates and will be validated through field pilots. The impact we aim for is to make scientific data usable not only by researchers but also by the small and medium-scale farmers most affected by climate change.

For development, we chose an architecture that requires no specialised hardware and runs in a web browser on any computer or phone. The system is built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript as a single file and requires no installation. We used Plotly.js for charts and Leaflet for interactive maps. For the 3D field model, the wind flow and the globe, we wrote our own 3D rendering engine without relying on external 3D libraries. NASA POWER data are accessed through its REST API and NASA GIBS imagery through its WMS service, while read-aloud and voice questions use the browser’s Web Speech API. Data are cached on the device, and the system is packaged as a Progressive Web App that can be installed on a phone like a native application. Our first prototype was developed in Python with Streamlit, and the 3D scenes in our demonstration video were modelled by our team in Python using NumPy and Pillow.

The creativity of the project lies in turning NASA data into an AI that reasons and communicates at the scale of an individual field, rather than simply visualising it. What distinguishes it from similar work is that the same digital twin speaks in two ways, one an engineer can use and one a farmer who cannot read can understand, that the AI explains its decisions step by step, and that each region has its own models built around the pests that actually threaten it.

Throughout development, our team paid particular attention to accessibility, which is why farmers enter no data and can use the system by voice in plain Turkish. We kept the cost at zero, since NASA data are free and the system needs no specialised hardware or subscription. We added caching and offline support with weak rural internet connections in mind. We reflected regional differences by building two sample farms, one in irrigated Çukurova and one in rain-fed Mardin Midyat. We protected privacy by ensuring that each farmer sees only their own field. Finally, we committed to transparency by stating the model’s limitations openly; the system itself notes, for example, that NASA POWER data use a grid of roughly 50 kilometres, and that soil moisture sensors and high-resolution satellite data will be added to reach parcel-level accuracy.
